strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: The private nanny becomes one of the best-paid hires in the house, and the qualified candidate is now the scarcest of all
lead.standfirst: Salary guides for 2026 place senior career nannies in ultra-wealthy households on pay that rivals the estate manager, and the shortage of trained candidates is the tightest in private service.
lead.body:
For a generation the private nanny sat quietly below the principal roles of the household. That order has been overturned. The salary surveys published for 2026 place senior career nannies working for ultra-high-net-worth families on packages of £95,000 to £140,000 and above, a band that now overlaps with the estate manager and the head of house. The Norland-trained nanny, long the benchmark of the profession, has become one of the most sought-after and most expensive hires a family can make.

The wider market sits a step below that ceiling but has still moved sharply. Most experienced nannies in the United Kingdom now earn between £50,000 and £80,000 a year, with newly qualified live-in roles in London and the South East starting from £40,000 to £55,000. The top of the range, from £120,000 upwards, is reserved for rota and international positions, where two nannies rotate weeks so the household is never uncovered, and where the successful candidate is expected to travel, to speak more than one language and to work seamlessly alongside security and the wider staff.

The pressure is a supply problem before it is a pay problem. The pool of formally trained, discreet, security-aware candidates grows slowly, and it is now being drawn abroad. Dubai and other low-tax jurisdictions are competing hard for English-speaking senior staff, offering tax-free packages and accommodation that a London family struggles to match on cash alone. The result is that families are paying more to recruit and, harder still, to retain.

For the house that gets it right, the nanny is not a peripheral hire but a figure at the centre of the family's trust, present in the most private hours of the day and often the longest-serving member of staff. Recruiting for the role, budgeting for it across several residences and holding on to the right person has become one of the defining tests of how well a modern household is run.
lead.why: For a house or estate manager, the nanny is now a senior recruitment, budgeting and retention challenge, not an afterthought, and a poor hire in the most trusted seat in the house is among the costliest mistakes a principal can make.

articles.title: A record 165,000 of the world's wealthy will move country this year, and the fortune now travels as a portfolio of passports
articles.body:
The Henley Private Wealth Migration Report for 2026 projects that 165,000 high-net-worth individuals will relocate internationally this year, a rise of 16 per cent on the record 142,000 moves recorded in 2025. The figure is the highest the survey has logged, and it confirms that the movement of private wealth across borders has become a permanent feature of the landscape rather than a reaction to any single event.

The destinations are familiar. The United Arab Emirates, the United States, Italy and Switzerland continue to absorb the largest inflows, while the United Kingdom remains the standout loser, shedding wealthy residents at a pace that policy has done little to slow. Most departing British millionaires are heading to those same four destinations, drawn by lighter tax, residence-by-investment routes and the sense of optionality that a second base provides.

The more telling shift is in how the wealthy now think about the move itself. Henley describes a change from the single relocation to the assembly of what it calls sovereign portfolios, collections of residence rights, citizenships and cross-border investments held so that a family can pivot quickly if circumstances change. The emphasis has moved from leaving one country for another to building resilience and contingency into the structure of the family's affairs.

For the people who serve these households, the consequence is concrete. A principal who holds rights in three or four jurisdictions expects the household to function across all of them, which means staff who can travel, who understand the paperwork of multiple residences and who can open, close and run a home at short notice wherever the family chooses to be.
articles.why: The internationally mobile family expects its household to move and operate across several jurisdictions, so multi-country fluency and readiness to travel are becoming baseline expectations of senior private staff.
articles.src: Henley & Partners, Private Wealth Migration Report 2026

articles.title: London's super-prime tenants set records, then press pause as the wealth-tax question hangs over the market
articles.body:
London's super-prime lettings market has just closed its strongest year on record. Agents report a financial year driven by repeat business and a globally diverse client base, with a flagship letting in prime central London agreed at £60,000 a week and landmark country houses changing hands at £14,000 to £17,000 a week. In the South West, one super-prime lettings desk lifted income by 45 per cent and deal volumes by 33 per cent over the same period.

The force behind the surge is tax. With buyers reluctant to absorb stamp duty and the prospect of a mansion tax, and with the abolition of non-domiciled status reshaping the calculus for internationally mobile residents, many of the wealthy have chosen to rent rather than own. Renting preserves the freedom to leave at short notice, and for a client whose plans may change with the next budget, that flexibility has been worth paying a great deal for.

Yet the same caution that fed the rental boom is now cooling it. In the first half of 2026 there were 17 per cent fewer lettings above £5,000 a week in prime central London than in the same period a year earlier. Agents attribute the slowdown to speculation about a possible wealth tax, which has prompted some internationally mobile tenants to hold back and wait for clarity before committing to a London base at all.

The swing from record activity to hesitation inside twelve months captures how quickly the top of the market now reacts to policy signals, and how provisional the presence of a wealthy household in any one city has become.
articles.why: When principals rent rather than buy, and treat a residence as temporary, the way a house is staffed, opened and closed changes, and the estate manager must run a portfolio built for mobility rather than permanence.
articles.src: Knight Frank, Rental Market Adjusts to Reforms and Future Tax Risks

articles.title: The Mediterranean charter season sells out at the top, and the family that books late finds the best hulls already gone
articles.body:
The Mediterranean charter market has tightened again for the summer of 2026, with weekly rates across the region expected to rise by 5 to 12 per cent depending on area and category. A yacht of 30 to 35 metres now commands roughly USD 35,000 to USD 65,000 a week, a 40 to 45 metre vessel USD 60,000 to USD 120,000, and a 50 to 55 metre yacht USD 100,000 to USD 200,000, before fuel, provisioning and taxes are added.

Geography still shapes the bill. France opens at around EUR 80,000 a week with 20 per cent VAT on top, Italy from a similar base with 22 per cent, while Greece and Croatia remain the softer entry points, with charters starting near EUR 15,000 a week under a 13 per cent rate. The gap has pushed a steady stream of demand towards the eastern Mediterranean, where value and cruising ground are easier to reconcile.

The defining feature of the season, however, is scarcity. Availability is tightening fastest for mid-size superyachts with generous beach clubs, water-toy packages and family cabin layouts, and July and August are expected to be almost fully committed for anything above 50 metres by early spring. The family that leaves its booking to the last moment now finds the strongest hulls long gone.

Crew is the quieter constraint behind the numbers. A Mediterranean-wide shortage of experienced crew pushed operating costs up by 15 to 20 per cent in recent seasons, and service quality varies more than it once did, so vetting the specific captain and chef has come to matter as much as choosing the yacht itself.
articles.why: The concierge or house manager who arranges a charter must now plan close to a year ahead and vet the crew as rigorously as the vessel, since a late booking or an unproven captain can undo the whole trip.

articles.title: Bordeaux offers a fine 2025 into a cautious market, and the collector weighs real quality against five years of falling prices
articles.body:
Bordeaux has released its 2025 vintage into one of the most testing markets in a generation. The wines themselves are widely admired, combining the depth of a warm year with freshness, polished tannins and lower alcohol, and the crop is one of the smallest in recent decades. On quality alone, 2025 is a vintage the serious cellar would want to own.

The difficulty is price. There is broad recognition across the trade that releases had to stay close to 2024 levels, with only modest increases at most, if the campaign was to sell at all. Most estates obliged. The conspicuous exception was Cheval Blanc, which released its 2025 futures at EUR 336 a bottle ex-négoce, up 20 per cent on the previous year, and which reached American shelves near USD 473 a bottle thanks to a weak dollar.

Early sales rose on the weak 2024 campaign, with leading merchants describing volumes as up a little, though still below the levels of five years ago. The secondary market gives the reason for restraint. The Liv-ex Bordeaux 500 index, a standard gauge of prices, fell 16.5 per cent over the five years to the end of May 2026, a decline that has taught buyers to treat en primeur as a question rather than a certainty.

With delivery of the 2025s not due until 2028, the collector is being asked to commit capital now for wine that will arrive in three years, into a market that has punished impatience. The vintage rewards those who buy for the cellar and the table, and tests those who buy for the ledger.
articles.why: Wine fluency is part of the private service repertoire, and the household that builds a cellar is judged on patience and timing as much as on the labels it chooses.
articles.src: Decanter, Bordeaux en primeur sales up a little

briefs.t: Business jet deliveries reach a 17-year high
briefs.b: New business jet deliveries jumped almost 15 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, with 162 aircraft handed over worldwide, and IBA forecasts more than 884 deliveries for the full year, up 6.5 per cent. Gulfstream led 2025 with 158 aircraft and USD 10.01 billion in billings, just ahead of Bombardier on 157.

briefs.t: UAE residents turn to contingency planning
briefs.b: Henley & Partners recorded a 41 per cent rise in enquiries from UAE-based individuals between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, with applications for alternative residence or citizenship up 29 per cent. The firm frames it as a phase of diversification and optionality rather than an exodus.

The 2026 private-staff salary guides show compensation pushing higher again across the top of the profession, with the largest rises falling to estate managers, Michelin-trained private chefs and senior career nannies. Competition from Dubai and other low-tax jurisdictions for English-speaking senior staff is a principal driver.
